title: SIEM export requirements and connector spec — customer templates & RBAC v2 mapping
content:
Executive summary:

This working doc captures the customer-facing requirements matrix and internal connector specification for SIEM exports (Splunk HEC, Datadog Logs, Azure Sentinel/Log Analytics) with focused notes on RBAC v2 mappings, audit-log schema, evidence automation, and operational acceptance tests. The goal is to produce a repeatable onboarding template and a minimal connector spec that engineering can implement and security can sign off on.

Audience: security, infra engineering, product security, customer success (onboarding).

Scope:
- Outbound export of Redwood audit and operational logs to customer SIEMs and vendor SIEM SaaS endpoints.
- Support for pushing events via HTTPS (HEC, Datadog HTTP intake, Azure Data Collector API), TLS syslog (RFC5424), and message-broker-based (Kafka) where customers require intermediate buffers.
- Not in scope: deep analytics queries inside customer SIEM; we only standardize event envelope and delivery semantics.

1) Customer requirements checklist (template to send to customers)
- Destination type: Splunk HEC / Datadog Logs / Azure Sentinel (Log Analytics Workspace) / TLS syslog / Kafka topic.
- Endpoint details: host, port, path, token or cert thumbprint.
- Preferred transport: HTTPS vs syslog/TLS vs Kafka.
- Expected throughput (events/min or tokens/min).
- Retention SLA target (how long they want raw logs retained).
- PII/PD/PHI filtering: fields that must be redacted at source and allowed redaction methods.
- Data residency constraints (which regions are allowed).
- Ingestion guarantees required: at-least-once vs at-most-once vs exactly-once (note: Redwood connectors support at-least-once; dedupe is a customer-side concern).
- TLS/mTLS requirement: none / optional / required (include CA and client cert details if mTLS).
- SIEM field mapping: customer to Redwood canonical field map (we provide a sample mapping CSV).
- RBAC roles needed on their side (if we need to create service principals or scoped API keys).
- Acceptable attack surface and IP allowlist: list of Redwood egress edges or VPC endpoints.
- Incident contact and escalation (email, phone, Slack channel).

2) RBAC v2 mapping (how Redwood roles map to connector privileges)
- Note: RBAC v2 is Redwood's internal role model introduced in 2024. For exports we use a small set of roles that control what categories of logs can be exported and which destinations are allowed.

Redwood role -> Allowed export scopes (example):
- security_audit_reader -> can export: auth.* events, rbac.* events, audit.action events. Cannot export: full request payloads, secrets fields.
- infra_ops -> can export: runtime.metrics, infra.* events, request-level performance logs. Not allowed: access to user PII fields.
- customer_support -> can export: support.case events, session metadata. Requires masking of user identifiers by default.
- admin_export -> can export everything including full_audit logs and evidence bundles. Requires additional approval (audit trail created).

RBAC enforcement notes:
- Connectors accept an internal service identity token scoped to a subset of export types. Tokens are minted by Redwood's control plane after verifying customer-approved RBAC mapping.
- Tokens include an "export_scope" claim (comma-separated string) and an expiry. Connectors validate scope before transmitting.

3) Audit log schema (canonical fields)
- Each event must be emitted as a single JSON object (UTF-8). Field list below is the canonical schema we require across SIEMs. Additional fields allowed but must be prefixed with "x_" to indicate non-standard fields.

Canonical fields (all lower_snake_case where possible):
- event_id: string (UUID v4).
- timestamp: ISO8601 UTC (e.g., 2025-02-10T15:23:01Z)
- service: string (redwood-hosted, control-plane, serving-runtime, console)
- environment: string (prod|staging|dev)
- severity: string (info|warning|error|critical|notice)
- event_type: string (auth.login, auth.fail, rbac.change, model.deploy, request.generate, embedding.create, billing.charge)
- actor: { type: string, id: string, name: string }  <-- NOTE: please see 'Content model constraints' below for serialization guidance.
- resource: { kind: string, id: string, name: string }
- request_id: string (UUID)
- client_ip: string (IP or empty)
- user_agent: string
- message: string (human-friendly summary)
- metadata: object (freeform)
- change_set: array (for configuration changes)

Content model constraints (for SIEM compatibility):
- Because many SIEMs flatten nested JSONs awkwardly, we require actor and resource to be serialized as dotted keys as fallback: actor.type, actor.id, actor.name, resource.kind, resource.id, resource.name. The top-level object must include both nested and flattened versions when feasible.
- Avoid binary fields; if evidence artifact is binary (e.g., screenshot) include a presigned URL (short-lived) in x_artifact_url and a checksum in x_artifact_sha256.

4) Evidence automation (how we surface audit evidence for compliance requests)
- Evidence bundles are generated on audit-demand or as a scheduled snapshot (configurable per customer). Bundles contain: the set of canonical events, associated artifacts (presigned URLs), RBAC approval trail, and a manifest.json describing the bundle.
- Delivery: bundles can be pushed to customer S3, Azure Blob, or shared via a short-lived signed URL.
- Automation triggers: API call from customer, scheduled cadence (daily/weekly), or triggered by compliance-run (e.g., quarterly SOC audit).
- Chain of custody: each bundle is stamped with a signed manifest (HMAC keyed with customer-specific secret) and logged in Redwood control-plane audit.

5) Connector specs (per target)
A) Splunk HEC (recommended for customers running Splunk Cloud/Enterprise)
- Protocol: HTTPS POST to /services/collector/event with HEC token in Authorization: Splunk <token> header.
- Format: JSON per HEC event; we send: { "time": <epoch_seconds>, "host": "<redwood-host>", "source": "redwood-audit", "sourcetype": "_json", "event": <canonical_event_json> }
- Batch mode: support batching up to 10MB payloads or 500 events per request, whichever hits first.
- Retry: exponential backoff with jitter; max retries 6. Use 429/503 handlers per Splunk guidance.
- TLS: TLS1.2+, optional mTLS when customer requests.
- Authentication rotation: support rotating HEC tokens with a grace window; connector will attempt dual-token sending during rotation.

B) Datadog Logs
- Protocol: HTTPS POST to https://http-intake.logs.datadoghq.com/v1/input with DD-API-KEY header.
- Format: array of JSON events. Each event should include "ddsource":"redwood" and "service":"<service>" in the payload.
- Rate shaping: Datadog enforces per-API-key limits; customers must provide expected throughput and we will gate client-side with a token bucket.
- Indexing considerations: we recommend attaching a "redwood_event_type" attribute to allow Datadog indexes to be created.

C) Azure Sentinel / Log Analytics
- Protocol: Azure Data Collector API (POST to https://<workspaceId>.ods.opinsights.azure.com/api/logs?api-version=2016-04-01) with shared key authorization.
- Format: JSON array of objects. Each object mapped to a custom log type (e.g., RedwoodAudit_CL). Field names must end with _s, _t, _d per Log Analytics best practices. We provide a mapping script that converts canonical field names to the _CL suffix naming convention.
- Authentication: support both workspace shared key and a managed identity push approach where customer sets up a service principal.

D) Syslog (TLS / RFC5424)
- Protocol: syslog over TLS (RFC5424).
- Message format: structured-data section contains a compact JSON blob under param "redwood"; avoid >8k messages. If event is large, send a summary and include x_artifact_url for full payload.
- Delivery: support both TCP and UDP transports but default to TCP+TLS for security.

E) Kafka (customer-managed)
- Protocol: SSL-enabled Kafka (SASL optional).
- Topic schema: events as UTF-8 JSON strings; key = event_id. Provide schema registry compatibility with Avro/JSON Schema on request.

6) Delivery guarantees and operational behavior
- At-least-once semantics by default. Connectors persist events locally in ephemeral buffer (disk-backed queue) until HTTP 2xx response received.
- Duplicate suppression: connectors annotate events with redwood_delivery_attempt and last_delivery_ts. Customers should dedupe by event_id.
- Backpressure: connectors implement client-side rate limiting and will enter a pause/backoff loop if the upstream returns sustained 429/5xx.
- Monitoring: each connector exports internal metrics (success_count, failure_count, queue_depth, last_error, average_latency) to Redwood observability. Customers can optionally receive health pings.

7) Security considerations
- Never send secrets or raw API tokens in event payloads. All tokens should be stored in Redwood KMS and never emitted.
- PII redaction: customers specify fields to redact and whether to replace with stable pseudonym or remove entirely. Redaction occurs pre-export.
- Presigned URLs: default expiry = 1 hour; customer may request longer. All presigned URLs include read-only and are logged.

8) Sample event (canonical JSON)
{
  "event_id": "7b2b5c4e-9a2a-4e5c-8d2a-9b5f2b6d4c3f",
  "timestamp": "2025-02-10T15:23:01Z",
  "service": "control-plane",
  "environment": "prod",
  "severity": "info",
  "event_type": "rbac.change",
  "actor.type": "user",
  "actor.id": "u-1293",
  "actor.name": "asha.patel@redwood.ai",
  "resource.kind": "policy",
  "resource.id": "policy-42",
  "message": "RBAC policy updated via console",
  "request_id": "req-33b2f",
  "x_artifact_url": "https://s3.amazonaws.com/redwood-evidence/bundle-20250210.tar.gz?X",
  "x_artifact_sha256": "e3b0c44298fc1c14..."
}

9) Onboarding checklist (for customer success)
- Gather endpoint and auth details using the customer requirements checklist above.
- Confirm RBAC mapping and get signed approval from the customer's security owner.
- Create internal service identity and generate export token scoped to approved export_scope.
- Run test harness: send 100 sample events across all event_types requested. Capture ingestion metrics at the SIEM side.
- Verify field mapping, timestamp fidelity, and artifact access.
- Enable scheduled evidence bundle if requested.
- Schedule post-onboarding review 2 weeks after go-live to validate volume and error trends.

10) Acceptance tests (minimal)
- Schema adherence: send 50 events with canonical fields and assert they arrive and parse in the SIEM (field presence check).
- RBAC enforcement: attempt to export an event outside the export_scope and assert it is rejected or not sent.
- Presigned URL validation: ensure artifact URL is accessible for the configured TTL.
- Retry behavior: simulate transient 503 and assert connector retries and eventually succeeds within configured backoff window.
- Performance: sustained throughput at declared events/min with latency under X ms (customer-specific).

11) Known limitations and open questions
- Exactly-once delivery is not provided end-to-end; customers needing dedupe should assert event_id in their SIEM pipelines.
- Large binary artifacts are referenced via presigned URLs rather than embedded. This means evidence availability depends on object store TTL.
- Mapping freeform metadata into Log Analytics’ strict suffix schema is lossy; we provide a conversion helper but complex nested metadata may be flattened.

Next steps:
- Engineering: produce Splunk and Datadog connector skeletons and a shared delivery library for retries, backoff, encryption, and local buffering.
- Security: review RBAC v2 scope claim format and sign off on token minting flow.
- CS/Onboarding: finalize the customer requirements form and add to the onboarding playbook.

Notes / TODOs (working list):
- Add sample Kafka Avro schema to repo (ACTION: Jonah).
- Determine acceptable default presigned URL TTL for enterprise customers (ACTION: Priya).
- Add automated conformance test to CI that runs against Splunk Cloud dev instance (ACTION: Liam).

References:
- Splunk HEC docs: https://docs.splunk.com/Documentation/Splunk/latest/Data/UsetheHTTPEventCollector
- Datadog logs intake: https://docs.datadoghq.com/logs/log_collection/
- Azure Data Collector API: https://docs.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/logs/data-collector-api

End of working draft.
